## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 dev success on both seeds, so I can't yet tell a learning failure from a generalisation failure. The default recipe uses 4 PPO epochs over 131k steps, which may be too little data for a stream of fresh designs. Its gamma of 0.95 also gives little weight to the +1 exact-build bonus late in 6–33-step episodes. Following the program's round-1 split, I propose three candidates. (a) Recipe only: 2 epochs (about 243k steps), gamma 0.97, lambda 0.95. (b) Architecture only: a deeper residual 2D CNN with global-context (FiLM-style) injection and small-gain output initialisation, using the default recipe. (c) The two combined. Until dev success rises above 0, I'll rank by training success. With r near 1.3, (b) and (c) get about 25% fewer samples than (a), so comparing them shows the trade-off between depth and samples.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. They were the start net with 2 epochs, a residual FiLM CNN, and that CNN plus 2 epochs. So the agent is not learning at all, and generalisation is not yet the issue. Each run took only about 60–70 s, far under the 900 s cap. The binding limit is the FLOP-based sample count: 94k–229k steps, about 23–56 updates. Depth plus 2 epochs did not help. The fastest way to get more samples is ppo_epochs=1 with r≤1, which gives about 400k steps; smaller batches would also give more updates. Exact building needs a per-anchor answer to one question: does this brick land at layer z, with every footprint cell missing at z? That logic is identical at every layer. A network that shares weights across layers, with per-layer neighbour channels and footprint min/max pooling, should learn it from far fewer samples. This round tests that network under two recipes, plus a recipe-only control on the start net.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored 0 dev success and 0 training success, across 94k–426k steps, 1–4 epochs, gamma 0.95–0.97 and three architectures. All runs finished in under 160 s, so time is not the constraint. Because training success is also 0, the problem is learning itself. More samples alone (r2c1, 408k steps) did not help. A likely trap is the shaped reward. A 2x2 brick that covers 3 target cells and 1 extra still earns positive reward, and the -0.01 step cost favours big, sloppy bricks. Together with gamma 0.95, this rewards fast approximate filling over exact builds. The PoolHead's fixed max/min/avg summary may also be too coarse to test "every footprint cell is a target cell at the landing layer". This round tests three things: a longer horizon with sharper sampling (lower entropy) on the starting network (recipe only), learned convolutions shaped to each brick footprint with global context, and a convolution plus attention model with global reasoning.

### Round 4
Nine trials have run, and all of them scored 0 on both dev success and training success. That includes runs with about 420k samples, gamma from 0.95 to 0.995, entropy from 0.002 to 0.01, 1 to 4 epochs, and four different network bodies (residual FiLM, layer-shared, footprint convolution, attention). Because training success never left 0, the problem is learning itself, and seed noise does not explain it. Every network so far shares one assumption: action index (t, y, x) is scored from the features at spatial cell (y, x), through a translation-equivariant per-cell head. If this world maps actions to cells differently (for example x and y transposed, swapped footprints, or a different anchor), then every such head ties a placement to the wrong place, and no recipe change would fix that. That fits the fact that the task warns the world may differ. The last round therefore tests action heads that learn the action-to-cell mapping themselves: a flat linear head, a hybrid of the per-cell and flat heads, and a plain MLP.
